q:
Given below are two statements followed by two conclusions. Taking the statements to be true, even if they seem to be at variance with commonly known facts, decide which conclusions logically follow.
Statement 1: All pens are tools.
Statement 2: Some tools are costly.
Conclusion I: Some pens are costly.
Conclusion II: Some costly things are tools.
Which one of the following options is logically correct?
options: Only conclusion I follows
Only conclusion II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow
Neither conclusion I nor conclusion II follows
solution:
Pens lie inside tools; the costly tools may lie entirely outside the pen region, so I is not forced (All + Some gives nothing definite).
"Some tools are costly" converts simply to "Some costly things are tools", so II follows.
Answer: only II.
Trap: assuming the costly tools must include a pen.

q:
Given below are two statements followed by two conclusions. Taking the statements to be true, even if they seem to be at variance with commonly known facts, decide which conclusions logically follow.
Statement 1: No river is a lake.
Statement 2: All lakes are ponds.
Conclusion I: Some ponds are not rivers.
Conclusion II: No pond is a river.
Which one of the following options is logically correct?
options: Only conclusion I follows
Only conclusion II follows
Either conclusion I or conclusion II follows
Neither conclusion I nor conclusion II follows
solution:
Every lake is a pond and no lake is a river, so the lake-ponds are ponds that are not rivers: I follows.
Ponds outside the lake region may still overlap rivers, so II is not forced.
Answer: only I.
Trap: "No + All" gives a "Some … are not" conclusion about the third term, never a universal "No".

q:
Given below are two statements followed by two conclusions. Taking the statements to be true, even if they seem to be at variance with commonly known facts, decide which conclusions logically follow.
Statement 1: Some kites are red.
Statement 2: All red things are bright.
Conclusion I: All kites are bright.
Conclusion II: Some kites are not bright.
Which one of the following options is logically correct?
options: Only conclusion I follows
Only conclusion II follows
Either conclusion I or conclusion II follows
Neither conclusion I nor conclusion II follows
solution:
The red kites are bright, so only "Some kites are bright" is certain.
Kites outside the red region may or may not be bright, so neither I nor II is certain on its own.
I and II have the same subject and predicate and are contradictory (All / Some-not): in every diagram exactly one is true.
Answer: either I or II.

q:
Given below are two statements followed by two conclusions. Taking the statements to be true, even if they seem to be at variance with commonly known facts, decide which conclusions logically follow.
Statement 1: No coin is a medal.
Statement 2: No medal is a trophy.
Conclusion I: No coin is a trophy.
Conclusion II: Some coins are trophies.
Which one of the following options is logically correct?
options: Only conclusion I follows
Only conclusion II follows
Neither conclusion I nor conclusion II follows
Either conclusion I or conclusion II follows
solution:
Two negative premises give no definite link between coins and trophies.
Coins may or may not overlap trophies, so neither I nor II follows alone.
I (No) and II (Some) are a complementary pair on the same two terms, so exactly one of them holds in every case.
Answer: either I or II.
Trap: choosing "Neither" without checking for a complementary pair.

Either conclusion I or conclusion II follows
solution:
The electric vehicles may all lie outside the bus region, so I is not certain.
"Some vehicles are electric" says nothing about electric things that are not vehicles, so II is not certain.
I and II are not about the same pair of terms, so "either" cannot apply.
Answer: neither I nor II.

Since doctors exist and all of them are voters, some voters are doctors (II, the conversion of I).
Answer: both I and II.

Statement 1: Some pencils are erasers.
Statement 2: All erasers are sharpeners.
Conclusion I: Some pencils are sharpeners.
Conclusion II: Some sharpeners are erasers.
Conclusion III: All sharpeners are pencils.
Conclusion IV: Some erasers are pencils.
Which one of the following options is logically correct?
options: Only conclusions I and II follow
Only conclusions I, II and IV follow
Only conclusions II and IV follow
All four conclusions follow
solution:
Pencil-erasers are sharpeners ⇒ some pencils are sharpeners (I ✓).
All erasers are sharpeners and erasers exist ⇒ some sharpeners are erasers (II ✓).
"Some pencils are erasers" converts to "Some erasers are pencils" (IV ✓).
III fails: sharpeners can extend well beyond the pencils.
Answer: I, II and IV.

Statement 1: No bird is a reptile.
Statement 2: Some reptiles are swimmers.
Conclusion I: Some swimmers are not birds.
Conclusion II: No swimmer is a bird.
Conclusion III: Some birds are swimmers.
Conclusion IV: Some reptiles are not birds.
Which one of the following options is logically correct?
options: Only conclusions I and IV follow
Only I and IV follow, and either II or III follows
Only conclusion IV follows
Only conclusions I, II and IV follow
solution:
The swimming reptiles are not birds ⇒ I ✓. No reptile is a bird and reptiles exist ⇒ IV ✓.
Swimmers outside the reptiles may or may not be birds, so II and III are each uncertain.
II (No swimmer is a bird) and III (Some birds are swimmers) are contradictory on the same two terms, so exactly one holds.
Answer: I and IV, and either II or III.
Trap: stopping at "Only I and IV".

Mangoes ⊂ fruits ⊂ healthy ⇒ I ✓, and hence III ✓ (mangoes exist).
II reverses an "All" ✗. IV fails because fruits and mangoes may be the same set.
Answer: only I and III.

III and IV fail: in one valid picture glasses ⊂ cups ⊂ mugs (with some mugs outside glasses), so glasses need not be outside cups; in another, glasses lie outside mugs.

Two negative premises give nothing about desks vs stools, so I and II are each uncertain.
I (No) and II (Some) are a complementary pair ⇒ either I or II.
Answer: either I or II, plus III and IV.

Neither conclusion I nor conclusion II follows
solution:
Keys ⊂ locks ⊂ doors, but the gate-doors may or may not include keys ⇒ neither I nor II is certain.
They are contradictory (Some / No) on the same terms ⇒ either I or II.

q:
Given below are three statements followed by two conclusions. Taking the statements to be true, even if they seem to be at variance with commonly known facts, decide which conclusions logically follow.
Statement 1: Some hills are rivers.
Statement 2: No river is a sea.
Statement 3: All seas are oceans.
Conclusion I: Some oceans are not rivers.
Conclusion II: Some hills are not seas.
Which one of the following options is logically correct?
options: Both conclusions I and II follow
Only conclusion I follows
Only conclusion II follows
Neither conclusion I nor conclusion II follows
solution:
Seas are oceans and no sea is a river ⇒ those oceans are not rivers (I ✓).
The hill-rivers cannot be seas ⇒ some hills are not seas (II ✓).
Answer: both.

q:
Given below are two statements followed by two conclusions. Taking the statements to be true, even if they seem to be at variance with commonly known facts, decide which conclusions logically follow.
Statement 1: All lions are cats.
Statement 2: Some cats are wild.
Conclusion I: Some lions being wild is a possibility.
Conclusion II: All wild animals being cats is a possibility.
Which one of the following options is logically correct?
options: Only conclusion I follows
Only conclusion II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow
Neither conclusion I nor conclusion II follows
solution:
A possibility holds unless the statements forbid it.
I: the wild cats may include lions — nothing forbids it ✓.
II: drawing the wild circle entirely inside cats keeps both statements true ✓.
Answer: both.

q:
Given below are two statements followed by two conclusions. Taking the statements to be true, even if they seem to be at variance with commonly known facts, decide which conclusions logically follow.
Statement 1: No ink is a paint.
Statement 2: All paints are colours.
Conclusion I: Some inks being paints is a possibility.
Conclusion II: All inks being colours is a possibility.
Which one of the following options is logically correct?
options: Only conclusion II follows
Only conclusion I follows
Neither conclusion I nor conclusion II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow
solution:
I is ruled out directly by "No ink is a paint" ✗.
II: put the ink circle inside colours but outside paints — both statements still hold ✓.
Answer: only II.

q:
Given below are two statements followed by two conclusions. Taking the statements to be true, even if they seem to be at variance with commonly known facts, decide which conclusions logically follow.
Statement 1: Some rings are gold.
Statement 2: No gold is silver.
Conclusion I: All rings being silver is a possibility.
Conclusion II: Some rings being silver is a possibility.
Which one of the following options is logically correct?
options: Only conclusion I follows
Neither conclusion I nor conclusion II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow
Only conclusion II follows
solution:
The gold rings can never be silver, so "all rings are silver" is impossible ✗.
Rings that are not gold may be silver ✓.
Answer: only II.
Trap: a "Some … are not" fact (some rings are not silver) kills the "All" possibility.

q:
Given below are two statements followed by two conclusions. Taking the statements to be true, even if they seem to be at variance with commonly known facts, decide which conclusions logically follow.
Statement 1: All dogs are pets.
Statement 2: No pet is wild.
Conclusion I: All pets being dogs is a possibility.
Conclusion II: Some wild animals being dogs is a possibility.
Which one of the following options is logically correct?
options: Only conclusion I follows
Only conclusion II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow
Neither conclusion I nor conclusion II follows
solution:
I: dogs and pets can be the same set ✓.
II: every dog is a pet and no pet is wild, so no dog is wild — impossible ✗.
Answer: only I.

q:
Given below are three statements followed by two conclusions. Taking the statements to be true, even if they seem to be at variance with commonly known facts, decide which conclusions logically follow.
Statement 1: Some tigers are leopards.
Statement 2: All leopards are jaguars.
Statement 3: No jaguar is a puma.
Conclusion I: Some tigers being pumas is a possibility.
Conclusion II: All tigers being jaguars is a possibility.
Which one of the following options is logically correct?
options: Neither conclusion I nor conclusion II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow
Only conclusion I follows
Only conclusion II follows
solution:
Definite: the leopard-tigers are jaguars, hence not pumas (some tigers are not pumas).
I: tigers outside jaguars may be pumas — not forbidden ✓.
II: put the whole tiger circle inside jaguars — all statements still hold ✓.
Answer: both.

q:
Given below are two statements followed by two conclusions. Taking the statements to be true, even if they seem to be at variance with commonly known facts, decide which conclusions logically follow.
Statement 1: All bats are mammals.
Statement 2: No mammal is a fish.
Conclusion I: All fish being bats is a possibility.
Conclusion II: Some mammals not being bats is a possibility.
Which one of the following options is logically correct?
options: Only conclusion II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow
Only conclusion I follows
Neither conclusion I nor conclusion II follows
solution:
I: bats are mammals and no mammal is a fish, so no fish is a bat — impossible ✗.
II: the mammal circle can be larger than the bat circle ✓.
Answer: only II.

q:
Given below are two statements followed by two conclusions. Taking the statements to be true, even if they seem to be at variance with commonly known facts, decide which conclusions logically follow.
Statement 1: Some songs are poems.
Statement 2: All poems are stories.
Conclusion I: Some songs are stories.
Conclusion II: All stories being songs is a possibility.
Which one of the following options is logically correct?
options: Only conclusion I follows
Only conclusion II follows
Either conclusion I or conclusion II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow
solution:
Song-poems are stories ⇒ some songs are stories (I ✓, definite).
II: draw stories (containing poems) entirely inside songs — both statements hold ✓.
Answer: both.

q:
Taking the following statements to be true, even if they seem to be at variance with commonly known facts:
Statement 1: Some cameras are lenses.
Statement 2: All lenses are glass.
Statement 3: No glass is plastic.
Which of the following conclusions logically follow from the statements?
options: Some cameras are glass.
Some cameras are not plastic.
No lens is plastic.
Some plastic things are cameras.
solution:
Camera-lenses are glass ⇒ (A) ✓; being glass they are not plastic ⇒ (B) ✓.
Lenses ⊂ glass and glass ∩ plastic = ∅ ⇒ (C) ✓.
(D): cameras outside the lenses may or may not be plastic ⇒ not certain ✗.

q:
Taking the following statements to be true, even if they seem to be at variance with commonly known facts:
Statement 1: All poets are writers.
Statement 2: Some writers are editors.
Statement 3: No editor is lazy.
Which of the following conclusions logically follow from the statements?
options: Some writers are not lazy.
Some poets are editors.
No poet is lazy.
Some editors are writers.
solution:
Editor-writers are not lazy ⇒ (A) ✓. (D) is the conversion of statement 2 ✓.
(B): the editor-writers may lie outside the poets (All + Some) ✗.
(C): poets who are not editors may be lazy ✗.

q:
Taking the following statements to be true, even if they seem to be at variance with commonly known facts:
Statement 1: No square is round.
Statement 2: All coins are round.
Which of the following conclusions logically follow from the statements?
options: All round things are coins.
No coin is a square.
Some round things are not squares.
Some squares are not coins.
solution:
Coins ⊂ round and round ∩ square = ∅ ⇒ coins and squares are disjoint: (B) ✓, and since squares exist, (D) ✓.
The coins are round things that are not squares ⇒ (C) ✓.
(A) reverses an "All" ✗.

q:
Taking the following statements to be true, even if they seem to be at variance with commonly known facts:
Statement 1: Some fans are coolers.
Statement 2: Some coolers are heaters.
Statement 3: All heaters are switches.
Which of the following conclusions logically follow from the statements?
options: Some coolers are switches.
Some fans are switches.
Some switches are heaters.
Some fans are heaters.
solution:
Cooler-heaters are switches ⇒ (A) ✓. Heaters exist and all are switches ⇒ (C) ✓.
Fans meet coolers only through "Some", and the fan-coolers need not be the heater-coolers ⇒ (B) ✗, (D) ✗.

q:
Taking the following statements to be true, even if they seem to be at variance with commonly known facts:
Statement 1: All rings are bands.
Statement 2: Some bands are wires.
Which of the following can be true, that is, is a possibility consistent with both statements?
options: All bands are rings.
No ring is a wire.
Some rings are not bands.
All wires are rings.
solution:
A statement is a possibility if at least one diagram satisfying both statements makes it true.
(A) rings = bands (then some rings are wires) ✓. (B) wire-bands outside the rings ✓.
(D) wires ⊂ rings ⊂ bands ✓.
(C) contradicts "All rings are bands" ✗.

q:
Taking the following statements to be true, even if they seem to be at variance with commonly known facts:
Statement 1: No apple is a berry.
Statement 2: Some berries are cherries.
Statement 3: All cherries are fruits.
Which of the following conclusions logically follow from the statements?
options: Some fruits are not apples.
Some cherries are not apples.
No apple is a cherry.
Some fruits are berries.
solution:
The berry-cherries are not apples ⇒ (B) ✓; they are fruits ⇒ (A) ✓ and (D) ✓.
(C): cherries outside the berries may be apples ⇒ not certain ✗.
Trap: extending "No apple is a berry" to all cherries.

q:
Taking the following statements to be true, even if they seem to be at variance with commonly known facts:
Statement 1: Not all managers are leaders.
Statement 2: All leaders are speakers.
Which of the following conclusions logically follow from the statements?
options: Some managers are not speakers.
Some speakers are leaders.
Some managers are leaders.
Some leaders are speakers.
solution:
"Not all managers are leaders" = some managers are not leaders.
Leaders exist and all are speakers ⇒ (B) ✓ and (D) ✓.
(A): the non-leader managers may still be speakers ✗. (C): managers and leaders may be disjoint ✗.

q:
Taking the following statements to be true, even if they seem to be at variance with commonly known facts:
Statement 1: All tulips are flowers.
Statement 2: Some flowers are blue.
Statement 3: No blue thing is edible.
Consider the conclusions:
(i) Some flowers are not edible.
(ii) Some tulips are blue.
(iii) Some tulips are not edible.
(iv) Some edible things are not blue.
(v) Some blue things are flowers.
The number of the above conclusions that logically follow from the statements is ________.
solution:
(i) blue flowers are not edible ✓. (iv) edible things exist and none is blue ✓. (v) conversion of statement 2 ✓.
(ii) and (iii): the blue flowers may lie outside the tulips, and tulips may be edible ✗.
Count = 3.

q:
Taking the following statements to be true, even if they seem to be at variance with commonly known facts:
Statement 1: No teacher is a banker.
Statement 2: All bankers are investors.
Statement 3: Some investors are traders.
Consider the conclusions:
(i) Some investors are not teachers.
(ii) No teacher is an investor.
(iii) Some traders are investors.
(iv) Some traders are not teachers.
(v) Some bankers are traders.
The number of the above conclusions that logically follow from the statements is ________.
solution:
(i) the bankers are investors who are not teachers ✓. (iii) conversion of statement 3 ✓.
(ii) investors outside bankers may be teachers ✗. (iv) the trader-investors may all be teachers (outside bankers) ✗.
(v) the trader-investors need not be bankers ✗.
Count = 2.

q:
Taking the following statements to be true, even if they seem to be at variance with commonly known facts:
Statement 1: All violins are strings.
Statement 2: All strings are instruments.
Statement 3: Some instruments are drums.
Consider the conclusions:
(i) All violins are instruments.
(ii) Some instruments are violins.
(iii) Some strings are drums.
(iv) Some instruments are strings.
(v) Some drums are instruments.
(vi) No violin is a drum.
The number of the above conclusions that logically follow from the statements is ________.
solution:
Violins ⊂ strings ⊂ instruments ⇒ (i), (ii), (iv) ✓. (v) converts statement 3 ✓.
(iii) and (vi): the drum-instruments may or may not meet the strings/violins ✗.
Count = 4.

q:
Taking the following statements to be true, even if they seem to be at variance with commonly known facts:
Statement 1: Some actors are singers.
Statement 2: No singer is a dancer.
Statement 3: All dancers are athletes.
Consider the conclusions:
(i) Some actors are not dancers.
(ii) Some athletes are not singers.
(iii) Some actors are athletes.
(iv) No actor is a dancer.
(v) Some athletes are dancers.
(vi) Some singers are not athletes.
The number of the above conclusions that logically follow from the statements is ________.
solution:
(i) singer-actors are not dancers ✓. (ii) dancers are athletes who are not singers ✓. (v) dancers exist and are athletes ✓.
(iii) actors may avoid athletes entirely ✗. (iv) actors outside singers may be dancers ✗.
(vi) singers may all be athletes (outside the dancers) ✗.
Count = 3.

q:
Statement: Some actors are poets.
Conclusion: Some actors are painters.
Which one of the following statements, if added to the given statement, makes the conclusion logically certain?
options: All painters are poets.
All poets are painters.
Some poets are painters.
No painter is a poet.
solution:
Need the actor-poets to be painters: "All poets are painters" puts every poet, including the actor-poets, inside painters ✓.
(A) is the reverse inclusion — poets may lie outside painters ✗. (C) Some + Some gives nothing ✗. (D) makes the actor-poets non-painters ✗.

q:
Statement: No manager is careless.
Conclusion: Some clerks are not managers.
Which one of the following statements, if added to the given statement, makes the conclusion logically certain?
options: All managers are clerks.
No clerk is careless.
Some clerks are careless.
Some careless people are not clerks.
solution:
With (C), the careless clerks cannot be managers ⇒ some clerks are not managers ✓.
(A): clerks could be exactly the managers ✗. (B) and (D) leave open that every clerk is a manager ✗.
Trap: (A) feels relevant because it links clerks and managers, but it allows clerks = managers.

q:
"If the match is cancelled, the tickets are refunded."
Based only on the above, which one of the following is necessarily true?
options: If the tickets are refunded, the match is cancelled.
If the tickets are not refunded, the match is not cancelled.
If the match is not cancelled, the tickets are not refunded.
The tickets are refunded only if the match is cancelled.
solution:
Statement: Cancel → Refund.
(B) is the contrapositive ¬Refund → ¬Cancel, which is equivalent ✓.
(A) and (D) are the converse Refund → Cancel; (C) is the inverse. Tickets may be refunded for other reasons ✗.

q:
"Whenever the alarm rings, Meera wakes up." On Tuesday, Meera did not wake up.
Based only on this information, which one of the following can be concluded?
options: The alarm rang on Tuesday.
Nothing can be concluded about the alarm on Tuesday.
The alarm rang on Tuesday but Meera ignored it.
The alarm did not ring on Tuesday.
solution:
Alarm → Wake. Wake is false, so Alarm must be false (if the alarm had rung she would have woken).
This is modus tollens, a valid form ⇒ the alarm did not ring.
(C) contradicts the rule; (B) ignores the valid contrapositive.

q:
"If Ravi studies, he passes." Ravi passed.
Based only on this information, which one of the following is correct?
options: Ravi studied.
Ravi did not study.
Whether Ravi studied cannot be determined.
Ravi studied and passed.
solution:
Study → Pass. Knowing Pass is true tells nothing about Study: Ravi may have passed without studying.
Concluding "Ravi studied" is the fallacy of affirming the consequent.
Both "studied" and "did not study" are consistent with the facts ⇒ undetermined.

q:
"Whenever the factory siren sounds, all workers leave the floor and switch off their machines."
If the above statement is true, which one of the following is not necessarily true?
options: If all workers have left the floor, the siren has sounded.
If some worker has not switched off the machine, the siren has not sounded.
When the siren sounds, all workers switch off their machines.
When the siren sounds, all workers leave the floor.
solution:
Let S = siren sounds, L = all leave, M = all switch off. Statement: S → (L and M).
(C) and (D) keep only part of the consequent — still true.
(B): not M ⇒ not (L and M) ⇒ not S (contrapositive) — true.
(A) is the converse L → S: workers may leave for lunch with no siren ⇒ not necessarily true.

q:
"If it does not rain, the match will not be postponed."
Which one of the following is logically equivalent to the above statement?
options: If it rains, the match will be postponed.
If the match is not postponed, it did not rain.
If the match is postponed, it rained.
If it rains, the match will not be postponed.
solution:
Statement: ¬R → ¬P. Contrapositive: flip and negate both parts ⇒ P → R: "If the match is postponed, it rained" ✓.
(A) R → P and (B) ¬P → ¬R (the same as A) are the converse/inverse ✗; (D) is unrelated.
Trap: negating only one part.

q:
"Ravi will go to the fair if and only if Sita goes."
Based only on the above, which one of the following is necessarily true?
options: If Sita does not go, Ravi does not go.
If Ravi goes, Sita does not go.
If Ravi does not go, Sita goes.
If Sita does not go, Ravi goes.
solution:
"If and only if" means both go or neither goes.
So if Sita does not go, Ravi does not go ✓.
(B), (C), (D) each allow exactly one of them to go, which the statement forbids.

q:
"If Anil gets the scholarship and clears the interview, he will join the institute." Anil did not join the institute.
Based only on this information, which one of the following must be true?
options: Anil did not get the scholarship.
Anil neither got the scholarship nor cleared the interview.
Anil did not clear the interview.
Anil did not get the scholarship, or did not clear the interview, or both.
solution:
(S and I) → J with J false ⇒ (S and I) is false.
¬(S ∧ I) = ¬S ∨ ¬I (De Morgan): at least one condition failed ✓.
(A) and (C) pick one particular failure; (B) demands both — none is forced.

q:
"If the server crashes, either the backup starts or an alert is sent." Today the backup did not start.
Based only on this information, which one of the following must be true?
options: The server did not crash today.
If the server crashed today, an alert was sent.
An alert was sent today.
If an alert was sent today, the server crashed.
solution:
C → (B or A) with B false reduces to C → A ✓.
(A): the server may have crashed with an alert sent ✗. (C): if there was no crash, no alert is needed ✗.
(D) is the converse of C → A ✗.

q: Which one of the following is the contrapositive of "If the shop is open, the lights are on"?
options: If the lights are on, the shop is open.
If the shop is not open, the lights are not on.
If the lights are not on, the shop is open.
If the lights are not on, the shop is not open.
solution:
Contrapositive of P → Q is ¬Q → ¬P: swap the parts and negate both.
(A) is the converse, (B) the inverse, (C) negates only one part.
Only (D) is equivalent to the original.

q:
S: "If a book is rare, it is costly."
(i) If a book is costly, it is rare.
(ii) If a book is not rare, it is not costly.
(iii) If a book is not costly, it is not rare.
Which one of the following is correct?
options: Only (i) is logically equivalent to S.
Only (ii) is logically equivalent to S.
Only (iii) is logically equivalent to S, and (i) is logically equivalent to (ii).
All of (i), (ii) and (iii) are logically equivalent to S.
solution:
S: R → C. (iii) ¬C → ¬R is its contrapositive ⇒ equivalent to S.
(i) C → R is the converse and (ii) ¬R → ¬C is the inverse; neither equals S.
But the inverse is the contrapositive of the converse, so (i) ≡ (ii).

q:
The statement "If Tara is selected, Uma is also selected" turned out to be false.
Which one of the following must be true?
options: Tara was selected and Uma was not selected.
Tara was not selected and Uma was selected.
Neither Tara nor Uma was selected.
Both Tara and Uma were selected.
solution:
An "if P then Q" statement is false in exactly one case: P true and Q false.
So Tara was selected and Uma was not ✓.
Trap: thinking a false conditional means "Tara not selected".

q:
"Every member of the chess club also plays carrom."
Based only on the above, which one of the following is necessarily true?
options: Anyone who plays carrom is a member of the chess club.
Anyone who is not a member of the chess club does not play carrom.
Anyone who does not play carrom is not a member of the chess club.
Only chess club members play carrom.
solution:
For any person: Chess → Carrom. Contrapositive: ¬Carrom → ¬Chess ✓ (C).
(A) and (D) say Carrom → Chess (converse); (B) is the inverse ✗.

q:
Fact: "If the bell rings, the class ends."
Consider: (i) The bell rings. (ii) The class ends. (iii) The bell does not ring. (iv) The class does not end.
Which one of the following combinations is not logically possible, given the fact?
options: (i) and (ii)
(i) and (iv)
(ii) and (iii)
(iii) and (iv)
solution:
Bell → End is violated only when the bell rings and the class does not end: (i) and (iv).
(ii) and (iii): the class may end for another reason ⇒ possible.
(iii) and (iv): nothing happens ⇒ possible.

q:
"If Arun cooks, dinner is late. If Bina cooks, dinner is late." Yesterday dinner was not late.
Based only on this information, which one of the following must be true?
options: Arun cooked yesterday.
Bina cooked yesterday.
Neither Arun nor Bina cooked yesterday.
Exactly one of Arun and Bina cooked yesterday.
solution:
Not late ⇒ (contrapositive of each rule) Arun did not cook and Bina did not cook ✓.
Any option in which one of them cooked would make dinner late.

q:
Consider the two statements:
"If the price rises, the demand falls." and "If the demand falls, the price does not rise."
If both statements are true, which one of the following must be true?
options: The price rises.
The demand falls.
The demand does not fall.
The price does not rise.
solution:
Suppose the price rises. Then the demand falls, and then the price does not rise — a contradiction.
So the price does not rise ✓ (P → ¬P forces ¬P).
With the price not rising, both rules hold whether demand falls or not ⇒ (B), (C) not forced.

q:
Each card has a letter on one side and a number on the other. Rule: "If a card has a vowel on one side, it has an even number on the other side."
Four cards lie on a table showing: E, M, 6, 3.
Which of the cards must be turned over to check whether the rule is being followed? (Select every card that must be turned.)
options: E
M
solution:
A card must be turned only if its hidden side could break the rule (vowel with odd number).
E: hidden side may be odd ⇒ turn. 3: hidden side may be a vowel ⇒ turn.
M: the rule says nothing about consonants. 6: an even number may have any letter behind it (the rule is not "even → vowel").
Trap: turning 6 is testing the converse.

q: Which one of the following is logically equivalent to "If it is a holiday, the bank is closed"?
options: It is a holiday only if the bank is closed.
The bank is closed only if it is a holiday.
If the bank is closed, it is a holiday.
If it is not a holiday, the bank is open.
solution:
"P only if Q" means P → Q (P cannot happen without Q).
So "It is a holiday only if the bank is closed" = Holiday → Closed ✓.
(B) and (C) are the converse; (D) is the inverse.
Trap: "only if" introduces the consequent, not the condition.

q:
"Clearing the written test is necessary for getting the job."
Based only on the above, which one of the following is necessarily true?
options: Clearing the written test guarantees the job.
Anyone who clears the written test gets the job.
Anyone who gets the job has cleared the written test.
Anyone who does not get the job has not cleared the written test.
solution:
"Q is necessary for P" means P → Q: Job → Written ✓ (C).
(A), (B) treat the necessary condition as sufficient (Written → Job) ✗.
(D) ¬Job → ¬Written is the same converse ✗.

q:
Scoring above 90 marks is sufficient for a merit certificate. Riya did not get a merit certificate.
Based only on this information, which one of the following must be true about Riya's score (in marks, out of 100)?
options: It was above 90.
It was exactly 90.
It was below 90.
It was not above 90.
solution:
Above 90 → Certificate. No certificate ⇒ (contrapositive) not above 90 ✓.
"Not above 90" includes exactly 90, so (C) "below 90" is too strong and (B) too specific.
Trap: treating "not above 90" as "below 90".

q:
"The flight will not take off unless the weather clears."
Based only on the above, which one of the following is necessarily true?
options: If the flight took off, the weather had cleared.
If the weather clears, the flight will take off.
If the flight did not take off, the weather did not clear.
Clearing of the weather guarantees that the flight takes off.
solution:
"Not T unless W" = "if not W, then not T" ⇒ contrapositive T → W ✓ (A).
Clear weather is necessary, not sufficient: (B) and (D) are the converse; (C) is the inverse.

q:
"A valid passport is necessary, but not sufficient, for international travel."
Based only on the above, which one of the following is necessarily true?
options: Everyone with a valid passport can travel internationally.
Some international travellers may not have a valid passport.
Anyone without a valid passport cannot travel internationally.
A valid passport is the only requirement for international travel.
solution:
"Necessary" means Travel → Passport; its contrapositive is ¬Passport → ¬Travel ✓ (C).
(A) and (D) make the passport sufficient, which the statement denies.
(B) contradicts "necessary".

q:
"Kiran will be promoted only if she completes the training."
Based only on the above, which one of the following is necessarily true?
options: If Kiran completes the training, she will be promoted.
If Kiran does not complete the training, she will not be promoted.
If Kiran is not promoted, she did not complete the training.
Completing the training is sufficient for Kiran's promotion.
solution:
"P only if T" = P → T. Contrapositive: ¬T → ¬P ✓ (B).
(A) and (D) are the converse T → P (training is necessary, not sufficient); (C) is the inverse.

q:
"Sunil goes for a walk unless it rains."
Based only on the above, which one of the following is necessarily true?
options: If Sunil does not go for a walk, it rained.
If it rains, Sunil does not go for a walk.
If Sunil goes for a walk, it did not rain.
Sunil goes for a walk only if it does not rain.
solution:
"W unless R" = "if not R, then W" (= R or W).
Contrapositive: ¬W → R ✓ (A).
(B), (C), (D) all claim rain stops the walk; the statement says nothing about rainy days.
Trap: reading "unless" as "if and only if not".

q:
"A student gets the medal if she tops the class, and only if she has full attendance."
Which one of the following correctly describes the conditions for getting the medal?
options: Topping the class is necessary and full attendance is sufficient.
Topping the class and full attendance are each both necessary and sufficient.
Topping the class is necessary.
Topping the class is sufficient and full attendance is necessary.
solution:
"M if T" = T → M: topping is sufficient.
"M only if A" = M → A: attendance is necessary.
Nothing says a medal requires topping, so (A), (B), (C) are not forced.
Trap: "if" and "only if" point in opposite directions.

subtopic: equivalent forms of a necessary condition
q:
"Without a ticket, no one is allowed inside the stadium."
Which of the following statements mean the same as the above statement?
options: Having a ticket is necessary to be allowed inside the stadium.
Having a ticket is sufficient to be allowed inside the stadium.
Anyone allowed inside the stadium has a ticket.
No one is allowed inside the stadium unless they have a ticket.
solution:
For any person: ¬Ticket → ¬Allowed, i.e. Allowed → Ticket.
(A) "necessary" = Allowed → Ticket ✓. (C) is the same ✓. (D) "not allowed unless ticket" = ¬Ticket → ¬Allowed ✓.
(B) Ticket → Allowed is the converse ✗ (a ticket-holder may still be refused).

q:
"Either a referral or a test score above 80 is sufficient for admission. Every admitted candidate must attend an interview." Neha was admitted.
Based only on this information, which one of the following must be true?
options: Neha attended an interview.
Neha had a referral.
Neha scored above 80.
Neha had a referral or scored above 80.
solution:
Admission → Interview, and Neha was admitted ⇒ she attended an interview ✓.
Referral and score are sufficient conditions, not necessary ones: Neha may have been admitted some other way ⇒ (B), (C), (D) not forced.
Trap: (D) treats "sufficient" as "the only ways".

q:
"No one can vote without being registered." Ali is registered.
Based only on this information, which one of the following is correct?
options: Ali voted.
Ali did not vote.
Whether Ali voted cannot be determined.
Ali must vote because he is registered.
solution:
Vote → Registered. Ali being registered (the consequent) gives no information about voting.
Registration is necessary, not sufficient ⇒ undetermined.

q: For a positive integer $n$, the condition "$n$ is divisible by 12" is ______ for the condition "$n$ is divisible by 4".
options: necessary but not sufficient
both necessary and sufficient
neither necessary nor sufficient
sufficient but not necessary
solution:
Divisible by 12 ⇒ divisible by 4 (12 = 4 × 3), so it is sufficient.
But 8 is divisible by 4 and not by 12, so it is not necessary.
Answer: sufficient but not necessary.

q: For a real number $x$, the condition "$x^2 > 4$" is ______ for the condition "$x > 2$".
options: necessary but not sufficient
sufficient but not necessary
both necessary and sufficient
neither necessary nor sufficient
solution:
If $x > 2$ then $x^2 > 4$, so $x^2>4$ is necessary for $x>2$.
But $x = -3$ gives $x^2 = 9 > 4$ with $x < 2$, so it is not sufficient.
Trap: forgetting negative values of $x$.

q:
Rules: "The lamp glows if and only if the switch is on and power is available." "Power is available whenever the generator runs or the grid supply is up."
Which of the following conditions, taken alone, are sufficient to guarantee that the lamp glows?
options: The switch is on and the grid supply is up.
The switch is on.
The switch is on and the generator runs.
The grid supply is up and the generator runs.
solution:
Lamp ⇔ (Switch ∧ Power), and (Generator ∨ Grid) → Power.
(A) Grid up ⇒ power; with the switch on ⇒ lamp glows ✓. (C) similarly via the generator ✓.
(B) power may be unavailable ✗. (D) the switch may be off ✗.

q:
"If you do not hurry, you will miss the bus."
Which one of the following is logically equivalent to the above statement?
options: If you hurry, you will not miss the bus.
If you miss the bus, you did not hurry.
Either you hurry or you miss the bus (or both).
You will miss the bus only if you do not hurry.
solution:
¬H → M is false only when you do not hurry and do not miss the bus; so it equals H ∨ M ✓.
(A) is the inverse; (B) and (D) are the converse M → ¬H. Hurrying does not guarantee catching the bus.

q:
"It is not true that Ajay and Vijay both passed."
Which one of the following is logically equivalent to the above statement?
options: Neither Ajay nor Vijay passed.
At least one of Ajay and Vijay did not pass.
Ajay passed but Vijay did not.
Exactly one of Ajay and Vijay passed.
solution:
¬(A ∧ V) = ¬A ∨ ¬V (De Morgan): at least one failed, possibly both ✓.
(A) is ¬(A ∨ V), too strong; (C) and (D) exclude the case where both failed.

q:
"Lina will not attend the meeting unless Mohan attends it."
Which of the following are logically equivalent to the above statement?
options: If Lina attends the meeting, Mohan attends it.
Lina attends the meeting only if Mohan attends it.
If Mohan attends the meeting, Lina attends it.
Either Mohan attends the meeting or Lina does not (or both).
solution:
"Not L unless M" = ¬M → ¬L = L → M.
(A) L → M ✓. (B) "L only if M" = L → M ✓. (D) M ∨ ¬L = L → M ✓.
(C) M → L is the converse ✗.

q:
"Whenever Priya travels by train, she carries a book."
Which one of the following is logically equivalent to the above statement?
options: Priya carries a book only when she travels by train.
If Priya carries a book, she is travelling by train.
If Priya is not travelling by train, she does not carry a book.
Priya never travels by train without carrying a book.
solution:
T → B is false only when she travels by train without a book; "never T without B" = ¬(T ∧ ¬B) = T → B ✓.
(A) and (B) are the converse; (C) is the inverse.

q:
"Either the meeting is postponed or the report is submitted today (possibly both)."
Which one of the following is logically equivalent to the above statement?
options: If the meeting is not postponed, the report is submitted today.
If the meeting is postponed, the report is not submitted today.
If the report is submitted today, the meeting is not postponed.
The meeting is postponed only if the report is not submitted today.
solution:
P ∨ R is equivalent to ¬P → R (and to ¬R → P) ✓.
(B), (C), (D) all say P and R cannot both happen, which the inclusive "or" allows.

q:
"You cannot enter the club unless you are a member or a guest of a member."
Based only on the above, which one of the following is necessarily true?
options: If you are a member, you can enter the club.
If you are neither a member nor a guest of a member, you cannot enter the club.
If you cannot enter the club, you are neither a member nor a guest of a member.
If you enter the club, you are a member.
solution:
"Not E unless (M or G)" = ¬(M ∨ G) → ¬E, and ¬(M ∨ G) = ¬M ∧ ¬G ⇒ (B) ✓.
(A) and (C) treat membership as sufficient; (D) ignores guests.

q: Which one of the following pairs of statements is not logically equivalent?
options: "If it is sunny, Ram plays." / "If Ram does not play, it is not sunny."
"Ram plays unless it is sunny." / "If it is not sunny, Ram plays."
"Ram plays only if it is sunny." / "If it is sunny, Ram plays."
"It is not the case that it is sunny and Ram plays." / "If it is sunny, Ram does not play."
solution:
(A) S → P and its contrapositive ✓ equivalent.
(B) "P unless S" = ¬S → P ✓ equivalent.
(C) "P only if S" = P → S, but the second is S → P (converse) ✗ not equivalent.
(D) ¬(S ∧ P) = ¬S ∨ ¬P = S → ¬P ✓ equivalent.

q:
"Neither the manager nor the clerk was present."
Which one of the following is logically equivalent to the above statement?
options: The manager or the clerk was absent.
It is not true that both the manager and the clerk were present.
If the manager was absent, the clerk was present.
The manager was absent and the clerk was absent.
solution:
"Neither M nor C" = ¬M ∧ ¬C = ¬(M ∨ C) ✓ (D).
(A) and (B) are ¬M ∨ ¬C, which is weaker (true even if one was present).

q:
"If Asha passes, then if Bina passes, Chetan will also pass."
Which one of the following is logically equivalent to the above statement?
options: If Asha passes or Bina passes, Chetan passes.
If Chetan passes, Asha and Bina both pass.
If Asha and Bina both pass, Chetan passes.
If Asha passes, then Bina passes and Chetan passes.
solution:
A → (B → C) is false only when A and B are true and C is false — exactly when (A ∧ B) → C is false ✓.
(A) also forces C when only one passes ✗. (B) is a converse ✗. (D) forces Bina to pass whenever Asha does ✗.

q:
"Gopal will be fined if he parks here, unless he has a permit."
Which of the following are logically equivalent to the above statement?
options: If Gopal parks here without a permit, he will be fined.
If Gopal has a permit, he will not be fined.
If Gopal parks here and is not fined, he has a permit.
If Gopal is fined, he parked here without a permit.
solution:
The statement is (Park ∧ ¬Permit) → Fine, i.e. ¬Park ∨ Permit ∨ Fine.
(A) is exactly this ✓. (C) (Park ∧ ¬Fine) → Permit is also ¬Park ∨ Fine ∨ Permit ✓.
(B) says a permit prevents any fine — not stated ✗. (D) is a converse ✗.

q: "All the trains that arrived today were late." If this statement is false, which one of the following must be true?
options: No train that arrived today was late.
At least one train that arrived today was not late.
Some trains that arrived today were late and some were not.
Exactly one train that arrived today was not late.
solution:
¬(all late) = at least one not late ✓.
(A) is too strong: one punctual train already makes the statement false.
(C) also claims that some were late — not forced. (D) fixes the number — not forced.

import itertools
def doms(k, maxn=4):
    for n in range(1, maxn + 1):
        yield from itertools.product(itertools.product((0, 1), repeat=k), repeat=n)
G = lambda D: not all(x[0] for x in D)
F = [lambda D: not any(x[0] for x in D), lambda D: any(not x[0] for x in D), lambda D: any(x[0] for x in D) and any(not x[0] for x in D), lambda D: sum(not x[0] for x in D) == 1]
W = [D for D in doms(1) if G(D)]
h = [L for L, f in zip('ABCD', F) if all(f(D) for D in W)]
assert len(h) == 1, h
ans = h[0]

q: "Some students in the class passed the test." If this statement is false, which one of the following must be true? (The class has at least one student.)
options: At least one student passed but not all.
All the students passed.
No student in the class passed.
Exactly one student did not pass.
solution:
"Some passed" means at least one passed. Its negation is "none passed" ✓.
(A) and (B) assert that someone passed, contradicting the negation; (D) fixes a count that depends on class size.

q: Which one of the following is the negation of "No bird in the cage can sing"?
options: All the birds in the cage can sing.
Some birds in the cage cannot sing.
Exactly one bird in the cage can sing.
At least one bird in the cage can sing.
solution:
"No bird can sing" is false exactly when at least one bird can sing ✓.
(A) is too strong; (B) is about birds that cannot sing; (C) is too specific.

q: Which one of the following is the negation of "Every student solved at least one problem"?
options: No student solved any problem.
Every student failed to solve at least one problem.
At least one student solved none of the problems.
Some student did not solve every problem.
solution:
Negation flips each quantifier and negates the inner part: ∀s ∃p solved(s,p) → ∃s ∀p ¬solved(s,p).
So some student solved no problem ✓.
(A) is too strong. (B) and (D) talk about a problem left unsolved, which is consistent with the original.

q: "There is a shop in the market that sells every brand of soap." If this statement is false, which one of the following must be true?
options: Every shop in the market fails to sell at least one brand of soap.
No shop in the market sells any brand of soap.
There is a shop in the market that sells no brand of soap.
Some brand of soap is not sold by any shop in the market.
solution:
Original: ∃shop ∀brand sells. Negation: ∀shop ∃brand ¬sells — every shop misses at least one brand ✓.
(B), (C) are too strong. (D) needs a single brand missed by all shops; shop 1 may miss brand X while shop 2 misses brand Y.
Trap: swapping the order of "every" and "some".

q: There are five lamps in a hall. The statement "At most two of the lamps are on" is false. Which one of the following must be true?
options: At least three lamps are on.
Exactly three lamps are on.
At least three lamps are off.
All five lamps are on.
solution:
"At most two on" means 0, 1 or 2 lamps on. Its negation: 3, 4 or 5 lamps on = at least three on ✓.
(B), (D) fix one value; (C) confuses on with off (at least three on means at most two off).

q: A building has four doors. The statement "Exactly one of the four doors is locked" is false. Which one of the following must be true?
options: Either no door is locked or at least two doors are locked.
No door is locked.
At least two doors are locked.
All four doors are locked.
solution:
"Exactly one" fails in two ways: fewer than one (none) or more than one (two or more) ✓.
(B) and (C) each cover only one of these cases; (D) is a special case.
Trap: negating "exactly one" as "none".

q:
"Not all the mangoes in the box are ripe."
If this statement is true, which of the following can also be true? (The box has at least two mangoes.)
options: No mango in the box is ripe.
Some mangoes in the box are ripe.
All the mangoes in the box are ripe.
Exactly one mango in the box is not ripe.
solution:
"Not all ripe" = at least one mango is not ripe; it leaves the rest open.
(A) all unripe ✓ possible. (B) some ripe, at least one unripe ✓ possible. (D) one unripe, the rest ripe ✓ possible.
(C) directly contradicts the statement ✗.
Trap: reading "not all are ripe" as "none is ripe".

Some applicant either is not a graduate or does not have a driving licence.

¬∀x (G ∧ L) = ∃x ¬(G ∧ L) = ∃x (¬G ∨ ¬L) ✓.

Some child in the group likes ice cream but not cake.
Some child in the group likes neither ice cream nor cake.

¬∀x (I ∨ C) = ∃x (¬I ∧ ¬C): some child likes neither ✓.
