q: Which one of the following pairs of statements can never both be true, but can both be false? (Assume there is at least one bag.)
options: "All bags are heavy." and "Some bags are not heavy."
"All bags are heavy." and "No bag is heavy."
"Some bags are heavy." and "Some bags are not heavy."
"Some bags are heavy." and "No bag is heavy."
solution:
(A) and (D) are contradictory pairs: exactly one is always true, so they can never both be false.
(C) can both be true (a mix of heavy and light bags).
(B) cannot both be true, but both are false when some bags are heavy and some are not ✓ (contraries).

q:
There are 7 boxes on a shelf. Both of the following statements are false:
"At most 3 of the boxes are empty."
"At least 5 of the boxes are empty."
The number of boxes that are not empty is ________.
solution:
First statement false ⇒ more than 3 empty ⇒ at least 4 empty.
Second false ⇒ fewer than 5 empty ⇒ at most 4 empty.
So exactly 4 are empty and 7 − 4 = 3 are not empty.

q:
"If Ajay goes, Bimal goes. If Bimal goes, Chitra goes. If Chitra goes, Deepa does not go." Deepa went.
Based only on this information, which one of the following must be true?
options: Ajay did not go.
Chitra went.
Bimal went.
Ajay went but Bimal did not.
solution:
Deepa went ⇒ Chitra did not go (contrapositive of rule 3) ⇒ Bimal did not go (rule 2) ⇒ Ajay did not go (rule 1) ✓.
Run the chain backwards using contrapositives.

q:
Six switches S1, S2, …, S6 obey the rules: if S1 is on then S2 is on; if S2 is on then S3 is on; if S3 is on then S4 is on; if S4 is on then S5 is on; if S5 is on then S6 is on. It is observed that S4 is off.
The number of switches that must be off is ________.
solution:
S4 off ⇒ S3 off (otherwise S4 would be on) ⇒ S2 off ⇒ S1 off.
Nothing forces S5 or S6 (a rule fires only when its "if" part is true).
Must be off: S1–S4 = 4.
Trap: also switching off S5, S6 (denying the antecedent).

q:
"If it is a weekday, Tina goes to office. When Tina goes to office, she takes the metro or the bus. Whenever she takes the metro, she reads a book." Today Tina did not read a book and did not take the bus.
Based only on this information, which one of the following must be true?
options: Today is a weekday.
Tina went to office by bus today.
Today is not a weekday.
Tina went to office today but did not read.
solution:
No reading ⇒ no metro (rule 3). No metro and no bus ⇒ she did not go to office (rule 2).
Not in office ⇒ not a weekday (rule 1) ✓.
(B) and (D) contradict the derived fact that she did not go to office.

q:
"If the dam overflows, the village floods. If the village floods, the school closes."
Based only on the above, which one of the following is necessarily true?
options: If the school is closed, the dam overflowed.
If the village does not flood, the school is open.
If the dam does not overflow, the school is open.
If the school is open, the dam did not overflow.
solution:
Chain: Dam → Flood → Close, so Dam → Close; contrapositive: Open (¬Close) → ¬Dam ✓.
(A) is the converse; (B) and (C) are inverses — the school may close for other reasons.

q:
"Pooja goes to the party only if Qadir goes. Qadir goes only if Ritu does not go. Ritu goes if Sohan goes." Sohan goes to the party.
Based only on this information, which one of the following must be true?
options: Pooja goes to the party.
Qadir goes to the party.
Pooja does not go to the party.
Ritu does not go to the party.
solution:
Sohan goes ⇒ Ritu goes ("R if S" = S → R).
Ritu goes ⇒ Qadir does not go (contrapositive of Q → ¬R).
Qadir does not go ⇒ Pooja does not go (contrapositive of P → Q) ✓.

q:
Five friends A, B, C, D and E were invited to a dinner. The following are known to be true:
If A attended, B attended. If B attended, C did not attend. If C did not attend, D attended. If D attended, E did not attend.
E attended the dinner. The number of friends who attended the dinner is ________.
solution:
E attended ⇒ D did not (rule 4, contrapositive).
D did not ⇒ C attended (rule 3, contrapositive).
C attended ⇒ B did not (rule 2, contrapositive) ⇒ A did not (rule 1).
Attended: C and E = 2.

q:
"If the exam is easy, Rohit passes. If Rohit passes, he gets a bike." Rohit got a bike.
Based only on this information, which one of the following is correct?
options: The exam was easy.
Rohit passed.
The exam was not easy.
Neither whether Rohit passed nor whether the exam was easy can be determined.
solution:
Easy → Pass → Bike. Bike is the final consequent; knowing it is true says nothing about the earlier links (affirming the consequent).
Rohit may have got the bike for another reason ⇒ both facts are undetermined.

q:
"If the team wins today, it qualifies. If it qualifies, it plays the final in Chennai. If it plays the final in Chennai, Kavya will watch the final. The team will not qualify if its captain is injured." Kavya did not watch the final.
Which of the following must be true?
options: The team did not win today.
The team did not qualify.
The captain was injured.
The team did not play the final in Chennai.
solution:
Kavya did not watch ⇒ no final in Chennai (D) ⇒ did not qualify (B) ⇒ did not win today (A).
(C): injury is one possible reason for not qualifying, but non-qualification does not prove injury (affirming the consequent of I → ¬Q) ✗.

q:
"Every member who attends the workshop gets a certificate. Everyone with a certificate can apply for the internship." Manoj attended the workshop.
Based only on this information, which one of the following must be true?
options: Manoj got the internship.
Manoj can apply for the internship.
Everyone who can apply for the internship attended the workshop.
Manoj did not get a certificate.
solution:
Workshop → Certificate → Can apply; Manoj attended ⇒ he can apply ✓.
(A) Being able to apply is not the same as getting the internship. (C) reverses the chain. (D) contradicts rule 1.

q:
"If Neel is in Delhi, Om is in Mumbai. If Om is in Mumbai, Pari is not in Pune. Pari is in Pune or Qasim is in Goa (or both)." Qasim is not in Goa.
Based only on this information, which one of the following must be true?
options: Om is in Mumbai.
Pari is not in Pune.
Neel is in Delhi.
Neel is not in Delhi.
solution:
Qasim not in Goa ⇒ Pari is in Pune (disjunctive syllogism).
Pari in Pune ⇒ Om not in Mumbai (contrapositive of rule 2) ⇒ Neel not in Delhi (contrapositive of rule 1) ✓.

q:
"If the generator fails, the lights go off. If the lights go off, the guard rings the bell. If the bell rings, the students leave the hall." The lights went off.
Based only on this information, which one of the following must be true?
options: The generator failed.
The generator did not fail.
The students left the hall.
The bell did not ring.
solution:
Lights off ⇒ bell rings ⇒ students leave ✓ (forward chain).
Nothing can be said about the generator: the lights may go off for other reasons ⇒ (A), (B) not forced. (D) contradicts rule 2.

q:
Seven lamps L1, L2, …, L7 obey the rule: for each $i$ from 1 to 5, if $L_i$ is on then $L_{i+2}$ is on. It is observed that L2 is on and L7 is off.
The number of lamps that must be on is ________.
solution:
Forward from L2: L2 on ⇒ L4 on ⇒ L6 on.
Backward from L7: L7 off ⇒ L5 off ⇒ L3 off ⇒ L1 off.
All seven states are fixed; lamps on: L2, L4, L6 = 3.

q:
"Every engineer in the firm knows Python. Everyone who knows Python has attended the bootcamp. No one who attended the bootcamp is a fresher."
Based only on the above, which one of the following is necessarily true?
options: Some freshers are engineers in the firm.
Everyone who attended the bootcamp is an engineer in the firm.
No engineer in the firm is a fresher.
Some people who know Python are freshers.
solution:
Engineers ⊂ Python-knowers ⊂ bootcamp attendees, and bootcamp ∩ freshers = ∅ ⇒ no engineer is a fresher ✓.
(A), (D) contradict this chain; (B) reverses an "All".

q:
"If the milk is boiled, it does not spoil by evening. If the milk does not spoil by evening, tea is served." The milk was boiled.
Based only on this information, which one of the following must be true?
options: Tea was served.
The milk spoiled by evening.
Tea was not served.
The milk spoiled but tea was served.
solution: Boiled ⇒ not spoiled ⇒ tea served ✓ (two applications of modus ponens).

q:
Argument: "All the drivers in this company are trained. Therefore, Rakesh is trained."
Which one of the following is an assumption required for the argument to be valid?
options: Every trained person in the company is a driver.
Rakesh is not a driver.
Rakesh is a driver in this company.
Rakesh works in this company.
solution:
The premise covers only drivers of this company, so the conclusion follows only if Rakesh is one of them ✓.
(D) is not enough: Rakesh may work there in another role. (A) is a converse; (B) cuts the link.
Negation test: if Rakesh is not a driver here, the argument collapses.

q:
Argument: "If the bridge is closed, traffic is diverted. Therefore, if the bridge is closed, the market is crowded."
Which one of the following, if assumed, makes the argument valid?
options: If the market is crowded, traffic is diverted.
If the bridge is not closed, the market is not crowded.
Traffic is diverted.
If traffic is diverted, the market is crowded.
solution:
Need a link from Diverted to Crowded so that Closed → Diverted → Crowded ✓ (D).
(A) is the wrong direction; (B) is about the bridge being open; (C) gives a fact, not a link.

q:
Statements: "If Varun gets the visa, he will travel in May. Varun will not travel in May unless his project ends."
Conclusion I: If Varun gets the visa, his project ends.
Conclusion II: If Varun's project ends, he will travel in May.
Which one of the following is correct?
options: Only conclusion II follows
Only conclusion I follows
Both conclusions I and II follow
Neither conclusion I nor conclusion II follows
solution:
Rule 2: "not T unless P" = ¬P → ¬T = T → P.
Chain: Visa → Travel → Project ends ⇒ I ✓.
II reverses T → P (the project ending is necessary for travel, not sufficient) ✗.
Answer: only I.

q:
"All the shops in Gandhi Lane are closed on Mondays." Today, Sai Stores, a shop in Gandhi Lane, is open.
Based only on this information, which one of the following must be true?
options: Today is not Monday.
Today is Monday.
Sai Stores is not in Gandhi Lane.
Whether today is Monday cannot be determined.
solution:
Shop in Gandhi Lane and Monday ⇒ closed. Sai Stores is in the lane and open ⇒ it is not Monday ✓ (modus tollens).
(C) contradicts the given information; (D) ignores the valid contrapositive.

q:
Statements: "Only employees with a badge can enter the lab. Some employees with a badge are interns."
Conclusion I: Some interns can enter the lab.
Conclusion II: Everyone who can enter the lab has a badge.
Taking the statements to be true, which one of the following is correct?
options: Only conclusion I follows
Only conclusion II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow
Neither conclusion I nor conclusion II follows
solution:
"Only badge-holders can enter" = Can enter → Badge ⇒ II ✓.
It does not say every badge-holder can enter, so the badge-holding interns may all be unable to enter ⇒ I ✗.
Answer: only II.

q:
Argument: "Every student who scored above 90 got a scholarship. Meena did not get a scholarship. So, Meena did not score above 90."
Which one of the following best describes the argument?
options: Invalid, because it denies the antecedent.
Valid, because the conclusion follows from the contrapositive of the first statement.
Invalid, because it affirms the consequent.
Valid only if Meena applied for the scholarship.
solution:
Rule: Above 90 → Scholarship. Given ¬Scholarship, the contrapositive gives ¬(Above 90) ✓ (modus tollens, valid).
No extra assumption is needed, so (D) is wrong; (A) and (C) name fallacies that are not used here.

q:
Argument: "If the shop has a sale, Leela buys shoes. The shop did not have a sale. So, Leela did not buy shoes."
Which one of the following best describes the argument?
options: Valid (modus ponens)
Valid (modus tollens)
Invalid (affirming the consequent)
Invalid (denying the antecedent)
solution:
Form: S → B, ¬S, therefore ¬B. This denies the antecedent and is invalid: Leela may buy shoes without a sale.
A truth-table row with S false and B true makes both premises true and the conclusion false.

q: Which of the following arguments are logically valid?
options: If it rains, the road is wet. If the road is wet, cars skid. So, if it rains, cars skid.
If Raju is hungry, he eats. Raju is eating. So, Raju is hungry.
The key is in the bag or in the car. It is not in the bag. So, it is in the car.
If the fan is on, the room is cool. The fan is off. So, the room is not cool.
solution:
(A) Hypothetical syllogism: P → Q, Q → R ⊢ P → R ✓.
(B) Affirming the consequent ✗.
(C) Disjunctive syllogism: P ∨ Q, ¬P ⊢ Q ✓.
(D) Denying the antecedent ✗.

q:
Statement: "In the survey, every respondent who owns a car also owns a two-wheeler."
Conclusion I: Every respondent who owns a two-wheeler owns a car.
Conclusion II: A respondent who owns no two-wheeler does not own a car.
Which one of the following is correct?
options: Only conclusion I follows
Neither conclusion I nor conclusion II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow
Only conclusion II follows
solution:
For each respondent: Car → Two-wheeler.
II is the contrapositive ✓. I is the converse ✗.
Answer: only II.

q:
Argument: "Whoever finishes the course receives a certificate. Ankit has received a certificate. So, Ankit finished the course."
Which one of the following, if added as a premise, makes the argument valid?
options: Ankit attended the course regularly.
Some who received a certificate did not finish the course.
Everyone who receives a certificate has finished the course.
Everyone who finishes the course receives a certificate on time.
solution:
As stated, the argument affirms the consequent (F → C, C ⊢ F) and is invalid.
Adding C → F (only finishers get certificates) makes it valid ✓.
(A) is unrelated; (D) repeats F → C; (B) points the other way.

q:
Statement: "The library is closed every Sunday."
Conclusion: "The library is open on every day other than Sunday."
Which one of the following is correct?
options: The conclusion does not follow; the statement says nothing about days other than Sunday.
The conclusion follows; it is the contrapositive of the statement.
The conclusion follows; it is the converse of the statement.
The conclusion does not follow, because the statement contradicts itself.
solution:
Statement: Sunday → Closed. The conclusion is ¬Sunday → ¬Closed, the inverse, which does not follow.
The library may also be closed on some other day (a holiday, say).
The contrapositive would be "If it is open, it is not Sunday".

q:
Statement: "Every multiple of 6 that appears on the list is circled." The number 18 is not circled.
Conclusion I: 18 does not appear on the list.
Conclusion II: Every circled number on the list is a multiple of 6.
Which one of the following is correct?
options: Only conclusion I follows
Either conclusion I or conclusion II follows
Only conclusion II follows
Neither conclusion I nor conclusion II follows
solution:
18 is a multiple of 6; if it were on the list it would be circled. It is not circled ⇒ not on the list ⇒ I ✓.
II is the converse of the rule ✗ (other circled numbers may not be multiples of 6).
Answer: only I.

q:
Argument: "If the company makes a profit this year, every employee gets a bonus. Sana did not get a bonus. Therefore, the company did not make a profit this year."
The argument depends on which one of the following assumptions?
options: Only employees get a bonus.
Sana is an employee of the company.
Every employee who gets a bonus works hard.
Sana's performance this year was poor.
solution:
Profit → (every employee gets a bonus). Sana not getting a bonus contradicts this only if Sana is an employee ✓.
If Sana is not an employee, her missing bonus says nothing about profit.
(A), (C), (D) do not connect Sana to the rule.

q:
"At least one of the three locks — red, blue and green — is open. The red lock is closed. The blue lock is open only if the red lock is open."
Based only on this information, which one of the following must be true?
options: The green lock is open.
The blue lock is open.
Only the red lock is closed.
The blue lock is open and the green lock is closed.
solution:
Blue open only if red open; red is closed ⇒ blue is closed.
Red and blue closed, and at least one is open ⇒ green is open ✓.

q:
Square grids are made with matchsticks of unit length: a 1 × 1 grid needs 4 sticks, a 2 × 2 grid needs 12 sticks and a 3 × 3 grid needs 24 sticks.
Continuing the same pattern, the number of matchsticks needed for a 10 × 10 grid is ________.
solution:
A $k \times k$ grid has $k+1$ horizontal lines and $k+1$ vertical lines, each made of $k$ sticks.
Sticks $= 2k(k+1)$: check $k=1,2,3$ gives 4, 12, 24 ✓.
For $k=10$: $2 \cdot 10 \cdot 11 = $ 220.
Trap: multiplying 4 sticks by 100 squares (shared sides counted twice).

q: A function $f$ defined on positive integers is observed to give $f(1) = 2$, $f(2) = 6$, $f(3) = 12$ and $f(4) = 20$. Assuming the simplest rule that fits all four observations continues, the value of $f(10)$ is
solution:
Differences: 4, 6, 8 (second difference constant 2) ⇒ quadratic. $f(n) = n(n+1)$ fits all four.
$f(10) = 10 \times 11 = 110$.
Trap: $n^2$ pattern guesses (100) or $(n+1)^2 - 1$-type slips.
verify:
import sympy as sp
n = sp.symbols('n')
pts = [(1, 2), (2, 6), (3, 12), (4, 20)]
poly = sp.interpolate(pts, n)
assert sp.degree(poly, n) == 2
ans = int(poly.subs(n, 10))

q: A sequence of dot patterns has 1 dot in Figure 1, 5 dots in Figure 2, 13 dots in Figure 3 and 25 dots in Figure 4. If the pattern continues in the same way, the number of dots in Figure 8 is
solution:
Increments: 4, 8, 12 — each figure adds 4 more than the previous one.
Continue: Figure 5: 41, 6: 61, 7: 85, 8: 113.
Formula: $2n^2 - 2n + 1$; $n = 8$: $128 - 16 + 1 = 113$.
verify:
import sympy as sp
n = sp.symbols('n')
poly = sp.interpolate([(1, 1), (2, 5), (3, 13)], n)
assert poly.subs(n, 4) == 25
ans = int(poly.subs(n, 8))

subtopic: induction: cellular rule with a cycle
q:
Nine bulbs are placed in a row. At the start only the 5th bulb is ON. In every step, all bulbs are updated together by the rule: a bulb is ON after the step if and only if exactly one of its neighbours was ON before the step (the two end bulbs have only one neighbour).
Writing 1 for ON and 0 for OFF, the row is 000101000 after Step 1 and 001000100 after Step 2.
The number of bulbs that are ON after Step 21 is ________.
solution:
Continue: Step 3: 010101010, Step 4: 100000001, Step 5: 010000010, Step 6: 101000101, Step 7: 000101000 = Step 1.
So the pattern repeats every 6 steps from Step 1.
$21 = 6 \times 3 + 3$ ⇒ Step 21 = Step 3 = 010101010 ⇒ 4 bulbs ON.
Shortcut: find the cycle instead of running 21 steps.
verify:
s = [0] * 9
s[4] = 1
hist = []
for _ in range(21):
    s = [1 if ((s[i - 1] if i > 0 else 0) + (s[i + 1] if i < 8 else 0)) == 1 else 0 for i in range(9)]
    hist.append(''.join(map(str, s)))
assert hist[0] == '000101000' and hist[1] == '001000100'
ans = sum(s)

q: A shaded equilateral triangle has area 64 cm². In Step 1, its sides' midpoints are joined and the middle one of the four smaller triangles is unshaded. In every later step, the same is done to every shaded triangle remaining. The total shaded area (in cm²) after Step 3 is
solution:
Each step keeps 3 of the 4 equal parts of every shaded triangle, so the shaded area is multiplied by 3/4.
After Step 3: $64 \times (3/4)^3 = 64 \times 27/64 = 27$ cm².
Trap: halving the area at each step, or using $(1/4)^3$.
verify:
from fractions import Fraction as Fr
tris = [Fr(64)]
for _ in range(3):
    tris = [a / 4 for a in tris for _ in range(3)]
ans = sum(tris)

q: A student evaluates $n^2 + n + 41$ for $n = 0, 1, 2, \dots, 5$, finds every value prime, and concludes that the expression is prime for every non-negative integer $n$. Which one of the following is correct?
options: The conclusion is correct for every non-negative integer $n$.
The conclusion is wrong; the smallest $n$ for which the value is not prime is 40.
The conclusion is wrong; the smallest $n$ for which the value is not prime is 41.
The conclusion is wrong; the smallest $n$ for which the value is not prime is 10.
solution:
Inductive generalisation from a few cases is not proof.
At $n = 40$: $40^2 + 40 + 41 = 40 \cdot 41 + 41 = 41^2 = 1681$, not prime.
For $n = 0$ to 39 the values are all prime (direct check), so 40 is the first failure.
Trap: spotting $n = 41$ (which also fails, since every term is divisible by 41) and missing 40.

q: Arun has observed several hundred swans in his life, and every one of them was white. Which one of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
options: It is probable, but not certain, that the next swan Arun sees will be white.
All swans in the world are white.
A swan that is not white cannot exist.
The next swan Arun sees will certainly be white.
solution:
Observations support an inductive generalisation, which is probable, not certain.
A single non-white swan would refute "all swans are white", so (B), (C) and (D) claim certainty that observation alone cannot give.

q: The total number of squares of all sizes in a 1 × 1, 2 × 2, 3 × 3 and 4 × 4 grid of unit squares is 1, 5, 14 and 30 respectively. Continuing the pattern, the total number of squares of all sizes in a 6 × 6 grid is

At a meeting, every person shakes hands exactly once with every other person. With 2, 3, 4 and 5 people the numbers of handshakes are 1, 3, 6 and 10. Following the same pattern, the number of handshakes with 12 people is
solution:
Each new person shakes hands with everyone already present: increments 2, 3, 4, …
Total for $n$ people $= n(n-1)/2$; for 12: $12 \times 11 / 2 = 66$.
Trap: $12 \times 11 = 132$ counts each handshake twice; 78 is for 13 people.
verify:
import itertools
ans = len(list(itertools.combinations(range(12), 2)))

q: Unit cubes are stacked to form a stepped pyramid: a 1-layer pyramid uses 1 cube, a 2-layer pyramid uses 5 cubes, and a 3-layer pyramid uses 14 cubes (each new bottom layer is a square one unit wider than the layer above it). The number of cubes in a 7-layer pyramid is ________.
solution:
Layer $k$ from the top is a $k \times k$ square of $k^2$ cubes.
7 layers: $1 + 4 + 9 + 16 + 25 + 36 + 49 = 140$.
verify:
layers = lambda L: sum(len([(i, j) for i in range(k) for j in range(k)]) for k in range(1, L + 1))
assert [layers(1), layers(2), layers(3)] == [1, 5, 14]
ans = layers(7)

subtopic: induction: which rule fits all observations
q: For inputs $x = 1, 2, 3, 4$ a machine outputs $y = 1, 3, 7, 15$ respectively. Which one of the following rules fits all four observations?
solution:
Check each rule on all four points:
$2x-1$: 1, 3, 5 ✗ at $x=3$. $x^2-x+1$: 1, 3, 7, 13 ✗ at $x=4$. $4x-5$: −1 ✗ at $x=1$.
$2^x - 1$: 1, 3, 7, 15 ✓.
Trap: accepting a rule after checking only the first two or three points.
verify:
obs = [(1, 1), (2, 3), (3, 7), (4, 15)]
R = [lambda x: 2 * x - 1, lambda x: x * x - x + 1, lambda x: 4 * x - 5, lambda x: 2 ** x - 1]
h = [L for L, f in zip('ABCD', R) if all(f(x) == y for x, y in obs)]
assert len(h) == 1
ans = h[0]

q: Fifty doors numbered 1 to 50 are all closed. Person 1 toggles (opens if closed, closes if open) every door; person 2 toggles every 2nd door (2, 4, 6, …); person 3 toggles every 3rd door; and so on until person 50 toggles door 50. The number of doors that are open at the end is ________.
solution:
Door $d$ is toggled once for every divisor of $d$. It ends open iff it has an odd number of divisors, i.e. iff $d$ is a perfect square.
Trying small cases shows doors 1, 4, 9 stay open — the squares.
Squares up to 50: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49 ⇒ 7.

q: Hexagonal tile patterns contain 1, 7, 19 and 37 tiles in Figures 1, 2, 3 and 4 respectively (each figure adds a complete ring of tiles around the previous one). The number of tiles in Figure 7 is
solution:
Ring $k$ adds $6(k-1)$ tiles: increments 6, 12, 18, …
Figure 5: 61, Figure 6: 91, Figure 7: 127.
Formula $3n^2 - 3n + 1$: $n = 7$ ⇒ $147 - 21 + 1 = 127$.
Trap: stopping at Figure 6 (91).
verify:
import sympy as sp
n = sp.symbols('n')
poly = sp.interpolate([(1, 1), (2, 7), (3, 19)], n)
assert poly.subs(n, 4) == 37
ans = int(poly.subs(n, 7))

q: A rumour spreads in a town. The number of people who know it is 3 on Day 1, 9 on Day 2 and 27 on Day 3, because each day every person who knows it tells two new people. Following the same pattern, the number of people who know the rumour on Day 5 is ________.
solution:
Each knower tells 2 new people, so the number triples every day: 3, 9, 27, 81, 243.
Day 5: $3^5 = $ 243.
Trap: adding 2 per person only to the new knowers.
verify:
k = 3
for day in range(2, 6):
    k = k + 2 * k
ans = k

q: Observe: $1 \times 9 + 2 = 11$, $12 \times 9 + 3 = 111$, $123 \times 9 + 4 = 1111$. Following the pattern, $123456 \times 9 + 7$ equals
solution:
The number of 1s in the result equals the number added: $+2 → 11$, $+3 → 111$, $+4 → 1111$.
So $123456 \times 9 + 7 = 1111111$ (seven 1s). Direct check: $1111104 + 7 = 1111111$.

q:
"It is not the case that if Arun studies, he will fail."
Which one of the following is logically equivalent to the above statement?
options: If Arun studies, he will not fail.
If Arun does not study, he will fail.
Arun studies and he does not fail.
Arun does not study or he fails.
solution:
¬(S → F) = ¬(¬S ∨ F) = S ∧ ¬F ✓.
(A) is a conditional — it is also true when Arun does not study, so it is weaker.
(D) is S → F itself, the opposite. Trap: negating a conditional into another conditional.

q:
"No pain, no gain."
Which one of the following is logically equivalent to the above statement?
options: If there is pain, there is gain.
If there is no gain, there was no pain.
Pain guarantees gain.
If there is gain, there was pain.
solution:
"No pain, no gain" = ¬Pain → ¬Gain; contrapositive: Gain → Pain ✓.
(A), (B), (C) all say Pain → Gain, the converse — pain is necessary, not sufficient.

q:
Policy: "A customer gets free delivery if the order is above ₹500 or the customer is a premium member; but there is never free delivery on Sundays." Kiran got free delivery on an order.
Based only on this information, which one of the following must be true?
options: Kiran's order was above ₹500.
Kiran's order was not placed on a Sunday.
Kiran is a premium member.
Kiran's order was above ₹500 or Kiran is a premium member.
solution:
Sunday → no free delivery; Kiran got free delivery ⇒ not Sunday ✓.
The policy gives sufficient conditions (above ₹500, premium) but does not say they are the only ways; so (A), (C), (D) are not forced.
Trap: (D) reads "if" as "only if".

q:
"If Ira wins, Jai loses. If Jai loses, Kabir wins. If Kabir wins, Ira does not win."
If all three statements are true, which one of the following must be true?
options: Jai loses.
Kabir wins.
Jai does not lose.
Ira does not win.
solution:
Chain: Ira wins → Jai loses → Kabir wins → Ira does not win. So "Ira wins" leads to its own negation ⇒ Ira does not win ✓.
With Ira not winning, the other two rules hold whether or not Jai loses ⇒ (A), (B), (C) not forced.

q: Which one of the following sets of statements is inconsistent, that is, the statements in it cannot all be true together?
options: Ravi is in Delhi. If Ravi is in Delhi, he is in India. Ravi is in India.
Ravi is in Delhi. If Ravi is in Delhi, he is in India. Ravi is not in India.
Ravi is not in Delhi. If Ravi is in Delhi, he is in India. Ravi is in India.
Ravi is not in Delhi. If Ravi is in Delhi, he is in India. Ravi is not in India.
solution:
Delhi → India. In (B), Delhi is true, so India must be true, but the set says Ravi is not in India — impossible ✓.
(C) and (D): with Delhi false the conditional holds whatever India is, so both are consistent. (A) is plainly consistent.

q:
"Every student in the hall is wearing a cap." Mohan is in the hall.
Given these, which one of the following statements cannot be true?
options: Mohan is wearing a cap.
Some people outside the hall are wearing caps.
Mohan is not wearing a cap.
Mohan is wearing a cap and a scarf.
solution:
Mohan is in the hall ⇒ he wears a cap, so "Mohan is not wearing a cap" contradicts the given facts ✓.
(B): the statement says nothing about people outside the hall. (A) and (D) are consistent.

subtopic: consistency of a set of conditionals
q:
Consider the statements:
(1) If the meeting is on Monday, Raj attends.
(2) If Raj attends, Sita does not attend.
(3) Sita attends if the meeting is on Monday.
(4) The meeting is on Monday.
Which one of the following is correct?
options: All four statements can be true together.
Statements (1), (2) and (4) cannot all be true together.
Statement (3) contradicts statement (1) on its own.
Statements (1), (2) and (3) together imply that the meeting is not on Monday.
solution:
From (1) and (2): Monday → Raj → ¬Sita. From (3): Monday → Sita. So Monday leads to both Sita and ¬Sita ⇒ (1)–(3) imply "not Monday" ✓.
Hence (A) is false (adding (4) is a contradiction).
(B): Monday, Raj attends, Sita absent satisfies (1), (2), (4). (C): Monday with both Raj and Sita attending satisfies (1) and (3).

q: Which one of the following sets of statements is consistent, that is, all statements in it can be true together? (Assume every class mentioned is non-empty.)
options: Some birds cannot fly. All birds are animals. No animal can fly.
All doctors are rich. No rich person is happy. Some doctors are happy.
No artist is lazy. Some lazy people are artists.
All cats are pets. Some cats are not pets.
solution:
(B): doctors ⊂ rich and rich ∩ happy = ∅ ⇒ no doctor is happy, contradicting "some doctors are happy".
(C): "Some lazy people are artists" is the contradictory of "No artist is lazy". (D) is a contradictory pair.
(A): take a world in which no bird (indeed no animal) flies — all three hold ✓. "Some … cannot" does not require that others can.

q: Which one of the following pairs of statements can never both be true? (Assume there is at least one shirt.)
options: "Some shirts are blue." and "Some shirts are not blue."
"No shirt is blue." and "Some shirts are not blue."
"Some shirts are blue." and "Not all shirts are blue."
"All shirts are blue." and "Some shirts are not blue."
solution:
"All shirts are blue" and "Some shirts are not blue" are contradictories — exactly one of them is true ✓.
(A) and (C) are both true for a mix of blue and other shirts; (B) both true if no shirt is blue.

q:
Three people make the following statements.
A: "B is lying."
B: "C is lying."
C: "A and B are both lying."
Each person either tells the truth or lies. For the three statements to be consistent, who is telling the truth?
options: Only A
A and C
Only B
Only C
solution:
Suppose A is truthful: then B lies, so C is truthful, so A and B both lie — contradicts A truthful.
So A lies ⇒ B is truthful ⇒ C lies. Check C: "A and B both lie" is false since B is truthful ✓.
Only B is truthful.

q:
Exactly two of Ana, Bo and Cy are selected for a team, subject to: "If Ana is selected, Bo is not selected" and "If Bo is not selected, Cy is selected".
Which one of the following must be true?
options: Cy is selected.
Ana is selected.
Bo is selected.
Ana and Bo are both selected.
solution:
Possible pairs: {Ana, Bo} breaks rule 1 ✗. {Ana, Cy}: Bo out ⇒ Cy in ✓ — consistent. {Bo, Cy}: rules not triggered ✓ — consistent.
Cy appears in both consistent teams ⇒ Cy must be selected ✓. Ana and Bo each appear in only one.

q:
"Every train to Mysuru stops at Mandya."
Which one of the following observations would show that this statement is false?
options: A train that went neither to Mysuru nor stopped at Mandya.
A train to Mysuru that did not stop at Mandya.
A train that stopped at Mandya but did not go to Mysuru.
A train to Mysuru that stopped at Mandya.
solution:
Mysuru → Mandya is broken only by a train with Mysuru true and Mandya false ✓.
(C) is a counter-example to the converse, not to the statement. (A) and (D) agree with it.

q:
In a class of 30 students, both of the following are true: "Some of the students wear glasses." "Not all of the students wear glasses."
Which one of the following is consistent with both statements?
options: Exactly 12 students wear glasses.
No student wears glasses.
All 30 students wear glasses.
The number of students who wear glasses is either 0 or 30.
solution:
"Some" ⇒ at least 1 wears glasses; "not all" ⇒ at most 29 do. Any number from 1 to 29 fits, e.g. 12 ✓.
(B), (C), (D) each break one of the statements.

q:
A list contains eight statements S1, S2, …, S8. For each $k$ from 1 to 8, statement S$k$ says: "Exactly $k$ of the statements in this list are false."
For the list to be consistent, exactly one statement must be true. The value of $k$ for that true statement is ________.
solution:
The statements contradict one another, so at most one is true.
If none were true, all 8 would be false, making S8 true — contradiction. So exactly one is true and 7 are false.
"Exactly 7 are false" is S7 ⇒ $k = $ 7.

q:
Points are marked on a circle and every pair of points is joined by a chord, with no three chords meeting at one interior point. With 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 points the circle is divided into 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 regions. A student predicts 32 regions for 6 points.
The actual number of regions for 6 points is ________.
solution:
Count with Euler's formula. For 6 points: chords $\binom{6}{2} = 15$; interior crossings $\binom{6}{4} = 15$ (each 4 points give one crossing).
Each crossing adds one region beyond the chords: regions $= 1 + 15 + 15 = $ 31.
Lesson: a pattern that fits five cases (doubling) can still fail — induction suggests, it does not prove.
